title: 307. Functions, Graphs & Transformations: Comparing Average Rates of Change
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Comparing Average Rates of a Linear Function
questions.learningObjective: Compare the average rates of change of a linear function on two intervals.
questions.question: For \(f(x)=2x+1\), compare the average rates of change on \([0,2]\) and \([2,4]\).

options.label: B
options.text: The average rate on \([0,2]\) is greater.

questions.explanation:
The average rate of change on \([0,2]\) is
\[
\frac{f(2)-f(0)}{2-0}=\frac{5-1}{2}=2.
\]
The average rate of change on \([2,4]\) is
\[
\frac{f(4)-f(2)}{4-2}=\frac{9-5}{2}=2.
\]
Both average rates are \(2\), so they are equal.
questions.hint: Use the average rate formula on each interval and compare the results.

questions.concept: Comparing Average Rates of a Quadratic Function
questions.learningObjective: Compare the average rates of change of \(f(x)=x^2\) on two intervals.
questions.question: For \(f(x)=x^2\), which interval has the greater average rate of change: \([0,1]\) or \([1,2]\)?
questions.explanation:
On \([0,1]\),
\[
\frac{f(1)-f(0)}{1-0}=\frac{1-0}{1}=1.
\]
On \([1,2]\),
\[
\frac{f(2)-f(1)}{2-1}=\frac{4-1}{1}=3.
\]
Since \(3>1\), the interval \([1,2]\) has the greater average rate of change.
questions.hint: Compute the average rate on each interval using the endpoints.

questions.concept: Comparing Average Rates of Two Functions
questions.learningObjective: Compare the average rates of change of two functions on the same interval.
questions.question: On the interval \([0,2]\), compare the average rates of change of \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(g(x)=3x\).
questions.explanation:
For \(f(x)=x^2\),
\[
\frac{f(2)-f(0)}{2-0}=\frac{4-0}{2}=2.
\]
For \(g(x)=3x\),
\[
\frac{g(2)-g(0)}{2-0}=\frac{6-0}{2}=3.
\]
Since \(3>2\), \(g\) has the greater average rate of change.
questions.hint: Calculate the average rate for each function on the same interval, then compare.

questions.concept: Comparing Average Rates from a Table
questions.learningObjective: Compare average rates of change from a table of function values.
questions.question:
The table gives values of \(f\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\
\hline
f(x) & 2 & 5 & 9 & 10
\end{array}
\]
Which interval has the greater average rate of change: \([0,2]\) or \([1,3]\)?
questions.hint: Use only the endpoint values of each interval from the table.

questions.concept: Comparing Average Rates of Quadratic and Linear Functions
questions.learningObjective: Compare the average rates of change of a quadratic and a linear function on the same interval.
questions.question: On the interval \([1,3]\), compare the average rates of change of \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(g(x)=2x+1\).
questions.explanation:
For \(f(x)=x^2\),
\[
\frac{f(3)-f(1)}{3-1}=\frac{9-1}{2}=4.
\]
For \(g(x)=2x+1\),
\[
\frac{g(3)-g(1)}{3-1}=\frac{7-3}{2}=2.
\]
Since \(4>2\), \(f\) has the greater average rate of change.
questions.hint: Evaluate each function at the endpoints of \([1,3]\), then apply the average rate formula.

questions.concept: Comparing Average Rates from Graph Points
questions.learningObjective: Compare average rates of change from points on a graph.
questions.question: The graph of \(f\) passes through \((0,0)\), \((2,6)\), and \((4,10)\). Which interval has the greater average rate of change: \([0,2]\) or \([2,4]\)?
questions.explanation:
On \([0,2]\),
\[
\frac{f(2)-f(0)}{2-0}=\frac{6-0}{2}=3.
\]
On \([2,4]\),
\[
\frac{f(4)-f(2)}{4-2}=\frac{10-6}{2}=2.
\]
Since \(3>2\), the interval \([0,2]\) has the greater average rate of change.
questions.hint: Use the \(y\)-coordinates of the given points as the endpoint values.

questions.concept: Comparing Average Rates of a Cubic Function
questions.learningObjective: Compare the average rates of change of \(f(x)=x^3\) on two intervals.
questions.question: For \(f(x)=x^3\), which interval has the greater average rate of change: \([-1,1]\) or \([0,2]\)?
questions.hint: Evaluate \(f(x)=x^3\) carefully at negative, zero, and positive inputs.

questions.concept: Comparing Average Rates of Exponential and Quadratic Functions
questions.learningObjective: Compare the average rates of change of \(f(x)=2^x\) and \(g(x)=x^2\) on \([0,3]\).
questions.question: On the interval \([0,3]\), compare the average rates of change of \(f(x)=2^x\) and \(g(x)=x^2\).
questions.explanation:
For \(f(x)=2^x\),
\[
\frac{f(3)-f(0)}{3-0}=\frac{8-1}{3}=\frac{7}{3}\approx 2.33.
\]
For \(g(x)=x^2\),
\[
\frac{g(3)-g(0)}{3-0}=\frac{9-0}{3}=3.
\]
Since \(3>\frac{7}{3}\), \(g\) has the greater average rate of change.
questions.hint: Compute both average rates exactly before comparing them.

questions.concept: Comparing Average Rates on Intervals of Different Lengths
questions.learningObjective: Compare average rates of change of a quadratic function on intervals of different lengths.
questions.question: For \(f(x)=x^2+1\), which interval has the greater average rate of change: \([0,2]\) or \([2,3]\)?
questions.explanation:
On \([0,2]\),
\[
\frac{f(2)-f(0)}{2-0}=\frac{5-1}{2}=2.
\]
On \([2,3]\),
\[
\frac{f(3)-f(2)}{3-2}=\frac{10-5}{1}=5.
\]
Since \(5>2\), the interval \([2,3]\) has the greater average rate of change.
questions.hint: The intervals have different lengths, so divide by the correct change in \(x\) each time.

questions.concept: Comparing Average Rates of Quadratic and Cubic Functions
questions.learningObjective: Compare the average rates of change of \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(g(x)=x^3\) on \([1,2]\).
questions.question: On the interval \([1,2]\), compare the average rates of change of \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(g(x)=x^3\).
questions.explanation:
For \(f(x)=x^2\),
\[
\frac{f(2)-f(1)}{2-1}=\frac{4-1}{1}=3.
\]
For \(g(x)=x^3\),
\[
\frac{g(2)-g(1)}{2-1}=\frac{8-1}{1}=7.
\]
Since \(7>3\), \(g\) has the greater average rate of change.
questions.hint: Evaluate both functions at \(x=1\) and \(x=2\), then compare the average rates.
